quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
quiz_item.question: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
options: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
choices: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Magnetic declination is the angular difference between true north (shown on the map) and magnetic north (where the compass needle points); failing to adjust for it causes significant navigation errors.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
options: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
choices: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Magnetic declination is the angular difference between true north (shown on the map) and magnetic north (where the compass needle points); failing to adjust for it causes significant navigation errors.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do index contour lines on an orienteering map differ from those on a standard topographic map?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do index contour lines on an orienteering map differ from those on a standard topographic map?
options: A. They are drawn as dotted blue lines to indicate seasonal water flow
B. They only appear at the exact summit of conical mountains
C. They are thicker to guide the eye but do not have elevation numbers printed on them
D. They point directly toward magnetic north across the map sheet
choices: A. They are drawn as dotted blue lines to indicate seasonal water flow
B. They only appear at the exact summit of conical mountains
C. They are thicker to guide the eye but do not have elevation numbers printed on them
D. They point directly toward magnetic north across the map sheet
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. They are thicker to guide the eye but do not have elevation numbers printed on them
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): On orienteering maps, index contour lines are thicker than intermediate contours to guide your eye, though they omit printed elevation numbers (p. 14).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: If your map does not have magnetic north-south lines drawn on it, how do you adjust a map bearing for magnetic declination?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: If your map does not have magnetic north-south lines drawn on it, how do you adjust a map bearing for magnetic declination?
options: A. Add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination
B. Subtract the degrees of error for both east and west declination
C. Multiply the contour interval by the magnetic variation angle
D. Point the direction-of-travel arrow south before rotating the bezel
choices: A. Add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination
B. Subtract the degrees of error for both east and west declination
C. Multiply the contour interval by the magnetic variation angle
D. Point the direction-of-travel arrow south before rotating the bezel
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): To convert from true north on the map to magnetic north on the compass, always add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination (p. 10).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When orienting a map using a compass, what do you do after setting the bezel to 360 degrees and placing the compass edge along a magnetic north-south line?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When orienting a map using a compass, what do you do after setting the bezel to 360 degrees and placing the compass edge along a magnetic north-south line?
options: A. Fold the map in half along the equator line
B. Turn the bezel until the orienting arrow points due east
C. Walk 100 paces forward while holding the map vertical
D. Rotate the map and compass together until the compass needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow
choices: A. Fold the map in half along the equator line
B. Turn the bezel until the orienting arrow points due east
C. Walk 100 paces forward while holding the map vertical
D. Rotate the map and compass together until the compass needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Rotate the map and compass together until the compass needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Rotating the map and compass together until the magnetic needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow aligns the map accurately with the surrounding terrain (p. 19).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How can you get the most accurate baseline measurement for your 100-meter walking or running pace?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How can you get the most accurate baseline measurement for your 100-meter walking or running pace?
options: A. Estimate your stride length indoors using a ruler and multiply by 100
B. Walk a 10-meter driveway once and multiply the result by 10
C. Cover the 100-meter course two or more times, especially on uneven ground, and divide total paces and time by total meters
D. Copy the pace count of another Scout who is approximately your height
choices: A. Estimate your stride length indoors using a ruler and multiply by 100
B. Walk a 10-meter driveway once and multiply the result by 10
C. Cover the 100-meter course two or more times, especially on uneven ground, and divide total paces and time by total meters
D. Copy the pace count of another Scout who is approximately your height
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Cover the 100-meter course two or more times, especially on uneven ground, and divide total paces and time by total meters
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Repeating the 100-meter course multiple times and averaging the total paces and minutes over the total distance provides a reliable baseline, particularly on uneven ground (p. 26).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why would an orienteer deliberately aim a few meters south of a control located along a north-south road?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why would an orienteer deliberately aim a few meters south of a control located along a north-south road?
options: A. To compensate for a broken compass bezel during the race
B. To guarantee that upon reaching the road, they know to turn north to find the control
C. To avoid having to punch the control card at that station
D. To add extra distance so their pace count reaches an even number
choices: A. To compensate for a broken compass bezel during the race
B. To guarantee that upon reaching the road, they know to turn north to find the control
C. To avoid having to punch the control card at that station
D. To add extra distance so their pace count reaches an even number
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. To guarantee that upon reaching the road, they know to turn north to find the control
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): This technique, called aiming off, ensures that when you hit the linear feature (the road), you know with certainty which direction to turn to reach the control (p. 38).

choices: A. Hang all control bags randomly in the woods and measure the distances afterward
B. Print control description sheets before selecting the park location
C. Invite competitors to start running while you place the markers ahead of them
D. Spend a half-day scouting the area with a notebook to note terrain, vegetation, features, and hazards
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Spend a half-day scouting the area with a notebook to note terrain, vegetation, features, and hazards

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: According to Orienteering USA rules, which of the following actions is prohibited for competitors in an orienteering event?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to Orienteering USA rules, which of the following actions is prohibited for competitors in an orienteering event?
options: A. Carrying a whistle for emergency signaling
B. Investigating the course before the event or using a GPS device for navigation
C. Using a thumb compass instead of a rectangular baseplate compass
D. Wearing long pants and gaiters to protect against brush and ticks
choices: A. Carrying a whistle for emergency signaling
B. Investigating the course before the event or using a GPS device for navigation
C. Using a thumb compass instead of a rectangular baseplate compass
D. Wearing long pants and gaiters to protect against brush and ticks
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Investigating the course before the event or using a GPS device for navigation
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Orienteering USA rules forbid pre-event investigation of the course and prohibit any navigational aid other than a compass during competition (p. 35).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: When teaching novice Scouts about 'handrails' on an orienteering course, which features serve as examples of more obscure natural handrails?
options: A. Paved parking lots and painted highway lane markings
B. Isolated single boulders in the middle of a flat meadow
C. Ridge lines, valleys, tree lines, forest fire burns, or avalanche scars
D. Magnetic north-south lines printed only on the border of the map
choices: A. Paved parking lots and painted highway lane markings
B. Isolated single boulders in the middle of a flat meadow
C. Ridge lines, valleys, tree lines, forest fire burns, or avalanche scars
D. Magnetic north-south lines printed only on the border of the map
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Ridge lines, valleys, tree lines, forest fire burns, or avalanche scars
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): While beginner courses use obvious trails or roads as handrails, more obscure natural handrails include ridge lines, valleys, tree lines, forest fire burns, and avalanche scars (p. 41).
